Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Seven percent. The battery icon is a sliver of angry red in the top corner of my screen. I leave the charger on the bed anyway. What’s the point? If I plug it in now, I’ll be three minutes late to the bar, and Sam is already looking for a reason to end this. *“Sorry I’m late,”* I’ll say, and he’ll do that slow blink he does when he’s tired. *“It’s fine,”* he’ll say, except his tone will mean: *You’re exhausting. We slept together twice, and suddenly you need constant reassurance. Let’s just go back to being friends.* And I won’t let him get away with that. I won’t just sit there and bleed quietly. I can feel the heat rising into my throat as I pull on my boots, my jaw clenching as I rehearse my counterattack. *“Oh, so I’m exhausting now? You were the one who kissed me last week, Sam! You don’t get to rewrite history and make me the crazy one just because you’re a coward!”* Yeah. *Coward.* That’ll hit him where it hurts. Because that’s what this silence over the last three days has been—cowardice. Just short texts. *Busy at work, talk soon.* No emojis. No *miss you.* Just a slow fade-out, preparing me for the guillotine. Honestly, screw him. I don’t even want to go tonight. By the time I’m locking my apartment door, I actively hate him. If he thinks he’s going to dump me over cheap draft beer, I’ll beat him to it. I’ll walk in, drop his sweatshirt on the table, and walk out. Protect the perimeter. Burn the bridge before he can strand me on it. I check my phone in the elevator. Six percent. The screen dims automatically to save power, casting my face in a ghostly, pathetic glow. *Stop it,* a quiet, clinical voice in the back of my head whispers. *You’re splitting. Remember what Dr. Bennett said? You’re writing the script before he’s even on stage. His firm is in the middle of an audit. He told you this on Monday.* I know that. I’m not an idiot. I know I’m doing the thing where I build a courtroom in my head and prosecute him for crimes he hasn't committed yet. Take a deep breath. In for four, hold for four— My phone buzzes. Five percent. It’s a text from Sam: *Got us a booth in the back! Ordered your favorite IPA so it’s waiting for you ❤️* A tidal wave of pure, intoxicating relief slams into my chest, knocking the wind out of me. My knees actually go weak as I step out onto the street. A heart emoji. A red one, not even the casual yellow one. And he remembered the IPA I like. God, I love him. He’s so good to me. How could I have thought those horrible things about him two minutes ago? I’m a monster. I’m broken, toxic, ungrateful— Wait. A booth *in the back*. The warmth evaporates, instantly replaced by ice water in my veins. Why the back? He usually likes sitting near the windows. You get a booth in the back when you want privacy. When you don’t want people to see someone cry. And ordering my beer ahead of time? That’s a classic speed-run tactic. That way, we don’t have to wait for the server. He can deliver the blow, pay the tab, and leave within twenty minutes. The heart emoji is just anesthesia before the amputation. *“I thought it would be easier to talk back here,”* phantom-Sam says in my head as I speed-walk down the pavement, the autumn wind biting my cheeks. *“You’re a great girl, Maya, really, I just think we crossed a line we shouldn’t have.”* *“A line?”* I hiss under my breath, earning a strange look from a guy walking a dog. *“I’m just a ‘line’ to you? A mistake you have to correct?”* My heart is hammering against my ribs like a trapped bird. I can already feel the humiliation of it, the crushing weight of being *too much* yet again. Everyone leaves. Everyone eventually sees the rotting floorboards beneath my feet and runs for the exit. Four percent. The screen is barely visible now. If my phone dies, how will I get an Uber home when I inevitably storm out in tears? I’ll be stranded. Alone and humiliated in the dark. I reach the heavy wooden door of the bar. My hand hovers over the brass handle. *This is your disorder talking,* the rational voice tries again, fainter now, drowned out by the roaring blood in my ears. *Just go in and see what’s actually happening.* I pull the door open, bracing for the execution. My eyes scan the dim room, locking onto the back corner. Sam is there. The second he sees me, his entire face transforms. The exhaustion of his workweek melts away, and he breaks into this huge, boyish grin that crinkles the corners of his eyes. He stands up instantly, opening his arms. I walk over on autopilot, my armor still spiked and heavy, and then he’s wrapping his arms around me, burying his face in the crook of my neck. He inhales deeply, holding me so tight my feet almost leave the floor. “God, I missed you,” he murmurs into my skin, his voice thick with genuine affection. “This week has been absolute hell. You have no idea how badly I needed to see your face.” He pulls back, kisses my forehead, and slides into the booth, pulling me down right beside him—not across from him. *Beside* him. His hand immediately finds my thigh under the table, warm and grounding, his thumb tracing slow, reverent circles on my jeans. It’s like heroin hitting my bloodstream. The terror vanishes, replaced by a dizzying, euphoric high. He’s here. He’s touching me. I am safe. I am wanted. I lean into his shoulder, drinking in the smell of his cedarwood cologne, feeling so fiercely, desperately in love with him that it aches. “I got us the back booth so I could actually hear you talk,” he says softly, smiling down at me. “And so I could do this.” He leans in and kisses me—slow, deep, and undeniably real. When he pulls away, my phone gives one final, weak vibrate in my coat pocket before the screen goes completely black. Dead. I look up at Sam’s warm, adoring eyes, and for three glorious seconds, there is peace. And then, I notice a tiny crease between his eyebrows. *Why is he holding me this tight?* the voice whispers, rising from the dark like smoke. *People only hold on this tight when they’re saying goodbye. It’s guilt. Did he meet someone else this week? Is he overcompensating?* His thumb is still rubbing my leg, a steady, loving rhythm. I smile back at him, picking up my cold glass of IPA, while inside my head, I’m already clearing my throat, stepping up to the microphone, and preparing my defense for the moment he lets go.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of borderline personality disorder and delivers a compelling first-person narrative that captures the exhausting cycle of catastrophic thinking and emotional dysregulation. The writer successfully executes the challenging task of showing the gap between internal catastrophizing and external reality. The narrative structure is well-crafted, moving from anticipatory dread through brief relief and back to suspicion in a realistic cycle. The use of the dying phone battery as a metaphor for the narrator's depleting emotional resources is subtle and effective. The piece excels at showing the physical manifestations of anxiety - weak knees, hammering heart, clenched jaw - which grounds the internal experience in visceral reality. The characterization is nuanced and authentic. Maya's voice remains consistent throughout, capturing both her self-awareness ("I know I'm doing the thing") and her inability to stop the destructive thought patterns. The brief appearances of Dr. Bennett and the clinical voice show she's in treatment, adding realism without heavy-handedness. The contrast between Maya's elaborate internal scenarios and Sam's genuine affection creates effective dramatic irony. His actual behavior - the heart emoji, remembering her beer preference, the enthusiastic greeting - directly contradicts her fears, yet she immediately finds new reasons for suspicion. This captures the relentless nature of the disorder perfectly. The prose is generally elegant and controlled, avoiding purple language while maintaining emotional intensity. The dialogue, though limited, feels natural and serves the story well. The piece maintains excellent pacing, building tension through Maya's spiraling thoughts before the relief of Sam's genuine warmth, then ending on the ominous note of her suspicion returning. The ending is particularly strong - the moment of peace followed immediately by new paranoia shows how the cycle perpetuates itself. This avoids false hope while demonstrating the exhausting nature of the condition. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the internal monologue becomes slightly repetitive, and some metaphors (like the "tidal wave" and "heroin hitting bloodstream") border on overwrought, though they remain within acceptable bounds for the emotional intensity being portrayed. + Physical-spatial: Blood Debt — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
"Blood Debt" Write a vivid third-person narrative depicting an unsanctioned underground duel between two talented but hot-headed martial artists. Their schools have been embroiled in a generations-old rivalry, and despite strict prohibitions from their masters, these two younger fighters arrange a secret confrontation fueled by personal pride and simmering animosity. - **One fighter** represents **Jigen-ryū**, a traditional, aggressive style practiced historically by elite samurai clans. Its practitioners emphasize explosive offense, decisive strikes, and overwhelming speed. Known historically for their arrogance and disdain toward outsiders, practitioners consider their art superior and untouchable. - **The opposing fighter** employs a form of historical **Piguaquan**, a Chinese martial art traditionally practiced by commoners, bodyguards, and street fighters. This style emphasizes whipping, circular strikes, rapid footwork, unpredictable angles of attack, and evasive maneuvers. Practitioners often come from lower social classes and view the traditional elite as pretentious and detached from true combat effectiveness. The fight takes place in the crumbling ruins of an abandoned temple, now functioning as a hidden arena for illicit duels. Passionate supporters from both factions surround them, wagering money, pride, and reputation on the outcome. **Essential Instructions:** Maintain absolute physical coherence throughout—clearly track fighters' positions relative to each other and their environment. Precisely depict strikes, counters, momentum shifts, and spatial dynamics, allowing readers to clearly visualize the mechanics and choreography of the fight at every moment. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A single pine torch sputtered in an iron bracket on the eastern pillar, its orange flame throwing violently elongated shadows across the ruined temple floor. The light barely reached the crumbling stone walls, where two distinct factions pressed inward, forming a jagged twenty-foot ring over the cracked flagstones. Coins clinked in the dark. Insults were spat in hushed, venomous tones. For three generations, the noble house of the Jigen-ryū and the dockside brotherhood of the Piguaquan had spilled blood in the alleys, and despite the strict truce signed by their aging masters, the youths had come to collect a debt of pride. At the northern edge of the ring stood Ren. Even without a blade, the Jigen-ryū heir carried the suffocating arrogance of the samurai class. He wore a dark, sleeveless training gi, his feet planted in a high, narrow stance, his left foot forward. He held his forearms vertical and parallel in front of his face, mimicking the famed *tonbo-no-kamae*—the dragonfly posture. His eyes were fixed on his opponent with cold disdain. Jigen-ryū did not believe in blocks; they believed only in a first strike so devastating that a second was unnecessary. Ten feet to the south stood Jin. Stripped to the waist, his lean torso glistening in the torchlight, the Piguaquan fighter looked like a street dog compared to a prized hound. He shifted his weight constantly, his stance wide and low, arms hanging loose at his sides like heavy ropes. He spat onto the dusty stones, his smirk mocking Ren’s rigid, aristocratic posture. Neither waited for a signal. Ren exploded forward. He drove off his rear right leg, crossing the ten-foot gap in two blindingly fast steps, his torso torquing as both hands rose above his right shoulder. A piercing, visceral scream—the *en-kiai*—ripped from his throat as he brought the edge of his right hand down in a vertical, bone-shattering chop aimed directly at the crown of Jin’s skull. Jin did not try to meet the force; doing so meant a broken arm. As Ren’s strike descended, Jin dropped his center of gravity and stepped forty-five degrees to his left—moving toward the western edge of the crowd, away from the torch. Ren’s hand cleaved the empty air where Jin’s head had been a millisecond prior, the sheer momentum pulling the Jigen-ryū fighter’s upper body downward. Already in motion, Jin pivoted on his left heel, his hips snapping clockwise. His relaxed right arm whipped upward from behind his back in a wide, vertical arc—a classic Piguaquan *pi* (chopping) palm. Because Ren was leaning forward at the end of his committed strike, his left flank was exposed. The heel of Jin’s open palm slammed into Ren’s floating ribs with the sound of a wet whip cracking against stone. Ren grunted, the impact driving him sideways toward the eastern pillar. Yet, true to Jigen-ryū’s relentless conditioning, he did not retreat to recover. As his right foot caught the flagstone to stop his lateral slide, just three feet from the flickering torch, he used the rebounding compression in his legs to launch himself straight back at Jin. There was no reset. Ren became a battering ram, driving forward in a tight linear path, unleashing a flurry of short, piston-like hammer-fists and vertical chops—the unarmed manifestation of *nuki-uchi*, continuous relentless slashing. Jin was forced onto the defensive, backpedaling toward the southern wall of spectators. The Jigen-ryū strikes were terrifyingly heavy. Jin wove his torso left and right, using *gua*—upward deflecting motions with his forearms—to redirect the downward trajectory of Ren’s fists by mere inches. A grazing blow caught Jin’s left shoulder, numbing his arm down to the fingertips. His back heel brushed the boots of his own shouting supporters at the southern boundary. He was out of room. Seeing Jin pinned against the human wall, Ren raised his right elbow high, stepping in with his right foot to deliver a decisive, downward-driving elbow strike to the bridge of Jin’s nose. Trapped in the linear corridor of Ren’s assault, Jin dropped nearly to the floor in a deep crouch, sliding his left leg behind Ren’s advancing right ankle. Ren’s elbow smashed into the chest of a spectator behind Jin, missing its mark. Coiled near the flagstones beneath Ren’s high guard, Jin unleashed an upward-whipping backfist (*liao*) directly from the floor. The knuckles of his right hand snapped vertically into the underside of Ren’s jaw. Ren’s head snapped back, teeth clacking together, blood spraying into the torchlight. His momentum stalled. Before Ren could drop his weight to regain his base, Jin surged upward from his crouch. He kept his left foot hooked behind Ren’s right heel and rotated his entire body counterclockwise, swinging his left arm in a massive, horizontal reaping arc across Ren’s chest. With his forward momentum halted and his base trapped, Ren’s feet left the ground. He crashed heavily onto his back in the center of the ring, kicking up a cloud of grey dust. A roar erupted from the Piguaquan faction, coins already changing hands in the shadows. Jin did not pause to gloat. As Ren hit the ground, his head oriented toward the northern wall and his feet toward Jin in the south, Jin leaped forward, spinning in the air to generate maximum torque. He brought his right heel down like an axe toward Ren’s exposed sternum. Even stunned, Ren’s ingrained samurai instincts took over. He rolled violently to his left—toward the western shadows. Jin’s heel shattered the brittle flagstone an inch from Ren’s ribs. Ren scrambled to one knee, facing east toward the torch, his breathing ragged, blood dripping from his chin. However, by rolling left, he had unwittingly moved directly into the path of Jin’s rotational momentum. Jin’s missed kick had planted his right foot firmly between Ren’s kneeling form and the southern crowd. Using that planted right foot as an pivot, Jin didn't pull back; he simply kept spinning clockwise. His arms extended fully, turning his body into a human windmill to generate whip-like centrifugal force. As his torso came around, his left palm slapped down on Ren’s frantically raised left forearm, pinning it against Ren’s chest. A split-second later, trailing the rotation of his hips, Jin’s right ridge-hand whipped horizontally through the gap in the defense. The strike caught the kneeling Jigen-ryū fighter cleanly across the left temple. The kinetic transfer was absolute. Ren’s eyes rolled back, the rigid tension vanishing from his frame instantly. He collapsed sideways onto the flagstones, sliding a foot into the dust before coming to a dead stop beneath the flickering orange glow of the torch. Silence fell over the ruins for a single, breathless heartbeat, broken only by the crackle of burning pine pitch, before the underground erupted into chaos.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional technical proficiency in martial arts choreography and spatial awareness. The author meticulously tracks every movement, position, and momentum shift throughout the fight sequence, fulfilling the prompt's most demanding requirement with remarkable precision. The combat flows logically from strike to counter-strike, with each fighter's positioning clearly established relative to the temple ruins, torch, and surrounding crowd. The characterization effectively establishes the class conflict through physical presentation and fighting philosophy rather than exposition. Ren embodies aristocratic rigidity and overwhelming offense, while Jin represents street-smart adaptability and evasive tactics. Their contrasting martial arts styles are authentically portrayed, with Jigen-ryū's linear aggression and Piguaquan's circular, flowing movements clearly differentiated. The prose maintains consistent quality throughout, employing precise technical language without becoming overly clinical. Phrases like "kinetic transfer was absolute" and detailed descriptions of specific techniques demonstrate deep martial arts knowledge while remaining accessible. The writing effectively balances action with atmospheric details - the sputtering torch, crumbling flagstones, and shadowy spectators create a vivid underground setting. However, the piece suffers from some predictable elements. The underdog street fighter defeating the arrogant aristocrat follows a familiar narrative arc. The ending, while technically well-executed, lacks emotional complexity or surprising developments. The characters, though clearly defined, remain somewhat archetypal without deeper psychological exploration. The pacing is relentless and appropriate for the subject matter, though this leaves little room for character development beyond their initial presentation. The violence is visceral but not gratuitous, serving the story's purpose of settling a "blood debt" between rival schools. The technical martial arts terminology is used accurately without overwhelming general readers, and the spatial choreography never becomes confusing despite the complex movements described. The author successfully creates a cinematic quality that allows readers to visualize each exchange clearly. + Physical-spatial: Breaking Formation — Score: 92.2
Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The digital clock above the floor-to-ceiling mirror bleeds a ruthless neon red: **00:14:22**. Fourteen minutes and twenty-two seconds left of the three-hour block, and my knee sleeves are soaked through with sweat that smells like fear and cheap laundry detergent. I am standing on the intersection of tape-line Four and letter C, the back-left anchor of a seven-man V-formation. In front of me, six boys in matching pristine black modal tees and immaculate €300 sneakers breathe in synchronized, shallow gasps. Their shoulder blades are pinched flat; their chins are tilted at an identical fifteen-degree angle toward the glass. And then there’s me. My oversized, bleach-stained hoodie clings to my back. Even in stillness, my posture betrays where I came from—pelvis slightly tucked, knees soft, weight hovering over the balls of my feet, waiting for a breakbeat that isn’t coming. Back home in the Bronx, stillness in the cypher was just coiled kinetic energy, a promise of violence or flight. Here, in the basement of Starlight Entertainment in Gangnam, stillness is submission. "Again," Director Kang says. He doesn't yell. He taps his polished oxford against the sprung marley floor. *Clack. Clack.* Kang is a legend—the choreographer who built the industry’s biggest boy bands out of raw cartilage and fear. When he scouted me at an international street battle in LA, I thought the scholarship was a golden ticket out of a dead-end zip code. I didn’t realize he hadn't bought my art; he’d bought my fast-twitch muscle fibers, fully intending to gut the house inside them. "From the second chorus transition," Kang commands, his Korean clipped, though he switches to heavily accented English when his eyes land on my reflection. "Marcus. Your *gak*—your angles—are dirty. You are melting the frame. Stop grooving. Execute." The track explodes from the corner subwoofers—a hyper-compressed, 130-BPM industrial synth-pop beat. *Five, six, seven, eight.* On *one*, we jump-split our feet to shoulder-width, simultaneously driving our right fists horizontally across our chests to land flush against our left deltoids, elbows locked parallel to the floor. Six fists hit with the unified *thwack* of a single rifle bolt closing. My fist arrives a millisecond late because my right shoulder automatically rolls forward first—a krump habit, loading the kinetic chain from the scapula to make the punch look heavy. In my world, you show the weight of the air you’re moving. Here, weight is a flaw. On *two*, we snap our heads ninety degrees to the left, toward the studio door, while dropping into a deep plié, knees tracking directly over the second toe, spine entirely vertical. My muscle memory rebels. As my hips drop, my lumbar spine naturally curves into a C-shape, my chest hollowing out in a classic hip-hop contraction. "Chest up, Marcus!" Kang barks over the snare. I jerk my sternum upright on the *and* count, throwing my center of gravity backward. I have to dig my heels into the marley to keep from stumbling as we hit *three-and-four*: a rapid double-isolation of the ribcage, shifting four inches right, four inches left, while our hands blade down to our thighs, fingers fused together. The clock ticks down: **00:11:05**. Now comes the travel. Counts *five* through *eight* require the V-formation to invert into an arrowhead, pushing me from the back-left corner (4-C) diagonally through the center traffic to the front-right wing (2-E). I push off my left foot, pivoting ninety degrees inward to slice between Ji-hoon (who is sliding backward down line B) and Min-seo (who is cutting horizontally across line 3). It’s a claustrophobic game of human Tetris. We are supposed to move via a low, skimming *bourrée*-style glide—hips completely level, heads trapped under an imaginary ceiling, arms crossed in an X over our throats. As I pass within three inches of Ji-hoon’s left shoulder, the heavy 808 bass drops. My body hears the sub-bass before my brain does. Instead of gliding flat across the floor, my ankles soften and I *skate* the transition—a Chicago footwork habit, rolling from the outside edge of my right sneaker to the ball of the foot, letting my hips sway laterally to absorb the transit. Because I dip an inch lower to catch the groove, my trailing left elbow swings out a fraction too wide. It grazes the sweat-slicked cotton of Ji-hoon’s ribs. Ji-hoon doesn’t flinch—he’s been trained here since he was twelve—but his eyes flick toward me in the mirror. Cold. Annoyed. The rich kid looking at the stray dog that tracked mud onto the rug. I hit mark 2-E on *eight*, dropping onto my right knee, left leg posted at a crisp ninety-degree angle, torso twisted forty-five degrees toward the mirror, left arm extended straight up like a lightning rod. In the mirror, six lightning rods pierce the ceiling. Mine has a bent wrist, my fingers splayed in a street-jazz tension, my chest heaving because I’m fighting my own tendons. Every fiber of my body wants to *waving* that energy up through the fingertips, to let the rhythm evaporate into the air. Instead, I have to choke it dead at the wrist. If I let them break me down to build me into a mannequin, I’ll get the debut contract. My mom’s rent gets paid. If I keep dancing like myself, I’m on a flight back to a neighborhood where boys like me don't get second acts. **00:08:40**. The music shifts to the bridge—half-time, heavy brass hits. We rise together on *one-two*, pushing through the front left heel, dragging the back right toe along the floor until our feet meet in a parallel first position. Counts *three-and-four* are pure tutting—geometric arm boxes framing the face. Right forearm rises vertically in front of the nose; left forearm snaps horizontally beneath the chin to form an L; both wrists hinge ninety degrees inward to create a closed box around the eyes. This, I know. I learned to tut on concrete steps, tracing the angles of apartment bricks. We hit the sequence—*tick, tick, clack*—our forearms folding and unfolding in synchronization. For two seconds, I am lockstep with them, my skin buzzing with the bizarre, terrifying high of erasing my own ego to become one cell in a seven-headed beast. Then comes the break on count *five*. A full-second pause before the final explosive chorus. The choreography dictates a sharp *dime-stop*—every muscle contracting simultaneously into concrete statues, hands dropped to our sides, staring dead-eyed into the glass as the synth rises to a shriek. My feet are glued to 2-E. My hands slice down to my thighs. I try to freeze. I can’t. The synth shriek has a filthy, syncopated triplet hidden underneath it, a ghost-note rhythm that begs to be caught. My chest betrays me first. On the *five-and*, my pectoral muscles fire a microscopic, violent pop—a classic West Coast hit—that sends a ripple down through my abs, unlocking my pelvis, which rolls backward and settles into a deep, defiant pocket on *six*. My chin tilts up, not at the prescribed fifteen-degree angle, but high, confrontational, looking Kang dead in his mirrored eyes. The music cuts. The silence in the studio is deafening, broken only by six boys exhaling in unison. The clock reads **00:08:12**. Kang walks forward. He stops directly in front of the mirror, blocking my reflection so I am forced to look at his actual face. He looks down at my feet—the frayed laces of my beat-up Jordans straddling the pristine white tape of 2-E—and then up to my chest, which is still subtly riding the phantom echo of the bassline. "You popped," Kang says softly. "The snare had a triplet behind it," I say, my voice raw, echoing off the glass. My thighs are trembling from the accumulated lactic acid, my heart hammering against my ribs. "The pause was dead. It needed a heartbeat." Around me, the other six trainees stay frozen in their dime-stops, terrified to break posture without permission. They are statues. I am flesh and blood, dripping onto the marley. Kang stares at me for five seconds. Ten. The red digits behind his head bleed down to **00:07:55**. I brace myself for the dismissal, already mentally packing my duffel bag. Instead, Kang turns to the soundboard operator. "Rewind thirty seconds," he orders in Korean. Then he looks back at me, his expression unreadable, cold as a scalpel. "Show me that hit again, Marcus. Slower. And the rest of you—watch his chest. If he can learn to lock his wrists, maybe you six can learn how to breathe." I drop back onto my right knee at 2-E, my palm flat against the floor, feeling the vibration of the room. I’m still trapped in the grid, still miles from home—but as the music cues up, I know my soul is still in my spine.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional technical mastery in fulfilling the prompt's demanding requirements. The author maintains meticulous spatial tracking throughout the choreography sequence, with precise positioning markers (4-C to 2-E), formation changes, and body mechanics that create a vivid kinetic map. The physical coherence is remarkable - every movement, from the synchronized fist strikes to the complex V-formation inversion, is rendered with surgical precision. The narrative voice authentically captures Marcus's cultural displacement through technical dance terminology that highlights the collision between street and commercial styles. The contrast between his natural "krump habit" and "Chicago footwork" against the demanded "bourrée-style glide" and rigid geometric precision creates palpable tension. The author skillfully uses muscle memory betrayals - the automatic shoulder roll, the lumbar spine curve, the chest pop - to externalize internal conflict. The characterization is nuanced and believable. Marcus's working-class anxiety manifests through concrete details (bleach-stained hoodie vs. €300 sneakers, his mother's rent) while his artistic integrity creates genuine stakes. Director Kang emerges as a complex figure - cold and exacting yet perceptive enough to recognize authentic talent. The other trainees are efficiently sketched through their synchronized perfection and class-conscious disdain. The prose maintains consistent voice throughout, balancing technical precision with emotional authenticity. The imagery is exceptionally vivid - the "neon red" clock bleeding time, the "claustrophobic game of human Tetris," the "ghost-note rhythm that begs to be caught." These descriptions serve the narrative rather than existing for their own sake. The emotional complexity is sophisticated, avoiding simple binaries. Marcus experiences both the "bizarre, terrifying high of erasing my own ego" and the compulsion to maintain his authentic voice. The ending strikes an earned balance - he hasn't won or lost, but found a precarious middle ground where his soul remains "in his spine" while still trapped "in the grid." The piece avoids common pitfalls of overwrought prose or unearned transformations. The resolution feels authentic - Kang's grudging recognition doesn't solve Marcus's fundamental dilemma but acknowledges his value. The technical dance terminology never becomes purple or pretentious, serving instead to highlight cultural collision. Minor weaknesses include occasional density that might challenge some readers, though this serves the claustrophobic atmosphere. The piece succeeds brilliantly at its ambitious goals, creating a kinetically precise, emotionally complex narrative that honors both street dance culture and the brutal precision of K-pop training. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 82.8
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The stone bench was cold, the docket was long, and Dream of the Endless had a headache. He rested his chin on a pale hand, his dark coat pooling around the base of his throne like spilled ink. Before him, the courtroom of the Dreaming shifted slightly—walls of grey marble occasionally bleeding into stained glass, then back again, depending on the mood of the gallery. At the moment, the gallery was bored. "Case four-seven-two," Lucien read from a scroll that appeared to have no end. The librarian adjusted his spectacles. "A territorial dispute in the subconscious of one Maximilian Sterling, age fourteen. *First Love v. Mora*." Dream’s starry eyes shifted slowly toward the two figures standing behind the obsidian lecterns. "Proceed," he said. His voice was the rustle of dry leaves, though today it carried the distinct undertone of a magistrate who had missed his lunch. The entity known as First Love stepped forward. He looked like a Renaissance cherub who had reluctantly aged into a Victorian poet, all rosy cheeks, tousled curls, and a waistcoat the color of bruised peaches. He wrung his hands, bashful even in litigation. "My Lord," First Love began, his voice trembling with earnestness. "For six months, I have tended the boy's mind. I built a meadow. Bluebells, mostly, with a border of clover. I introduced an avatar of young Chloe Miller from his third-period algebra class. The lighting was permanently set to golden hour." "Get to the tort," Dream said. First Love swallowed. "It is a delicate engine, my Lord. A recurring narrative. They run. They laugh. She trips—gracefully—and pins him to the grass. Their faces draw close. His heart rate elevates to a healthy one-hundred-and-ten beats per minute, and he wakes in a state of pleasant, formative confusion. It is artisanal work." He shot a venomous glare across the aisle. "Until last Tuesday." From the defense lectern came a sound like dry twigs snapping in a dead forest. Mora was emits faint cackles that echoed uncomfortably through the vaulted ceilings. She was tall, draped in moth-eaten shawls, with hair like wet river-weeds and eyes a little too wide for her gaunt face. Yet, for all the corpse-like pallor, there was a sharp, predatory symmetry to her cheekbones. She leaned heavily on the podium, picking at her teeth with a long, grey thumbnail. "And what occurred on Tuesday?" Dream asked, though he already knew. He knew everything that happened here. The formality of the court was merely to keep the nightmares from eating the delusions in the hallways. "She hijacked the transition!" First Love cried, pointing an accusing, manicured finger. "Chloe pinned the boy, just as scripted. The dandelion seeds were floating on the breeze! And then—*she* phased in." "I didn't phase," Mora rasped, her Slavic accent thick as grave dirt. "I slid. The framing was already there. Girl on top of boy. Chest exposed. Honestly, Your Honor, he practically set the table for me." "You unhinged your jaw," First Love whispered, horrified. "You turned a moment of burgeoning adolescent tenderness into sleep paralysis. You sat on his sternum and crushed the breath from his lungs!" Mora shrugged a bony shoulder. "A girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Dream pinched the bridge of his nose. "Mora. You have been assigned the barracks in Omsk and three suburban cul-de-sacs in Ohio. Why are you poaching in a fourteen-year-old’s meadow?" "Have you tasted Ohio lately, Lord?" Mora asked, leaning forward. "All anxieties about mortgage rates and lawn care. It’s dry. Like chewing sawdust. This kid, though?" She kissed her grey fingertips. "Pure, distilled hormone soup. Do you know how much kinetic energy a fourteen-year-old boy generates when he’s terrified *and* aroused? It’s like veal." First Love gasped, clutching his peach waistcoat. "It is an abomination! The boy woke up sweating, gasping for air, and—most disturbingly—he didn't want to leave the dream! You’ve crossed his wires! Yesterday in algebra, Chloe Miller dropped her pencil, and the boy looked at her neck to check for gills!" Mora let out another faint cackle. It bounced off the high stone arches, making several minor figments in the back row flinch. "He likes a woman who takes charge. What can I say? I have a certain *je ne sais quoi*." "You smell of stagnant marsh water!" "And yet," Mora said smugly, "when he fell asleep during history class today, guess who he was hoping would sit on his ribs?" "Silence," Dream said. He did not raise his voice, yet the word dropped the temperature in the room by ten degrees. He looked between them: the blushing architect of puppy love, and the ancient bog-spirit of suffocation. In truth, Mora was entirely in the wrong. The meadow was zoned for Class-B Romantic Whimsy. By rights, Dream should banish her back to the dark corners of the Slavic forests and scrub the boy's memory with a pleasant dream about finding twenty dollars. However. First Love had filed forty-two injunctions this month alone. He was pedantic, overly fond of soft focus, and frankly, his meadows were derivative. A bit of grit in the oyster, Dream mused, might actually produce a pearl. Or at least something mildly entertaining to watch. A tiny, almost imperceptible quirk touched the corner of the Dream King's pale mouth. "The Court recognizes the labor of the plaintiff," Dream intoned, sitting up straight. First Love puffed out his chest, victorious. "The meadow of Maximilian Sterling shall remain under the jurisdiction of First Love. The golden hour lighting is to be restored." "Thank you, my Lord," First Love sighed. "However," Dream continued smoothly, "the subconscious cannot be entirely sanitized. Mora has already taken root in the boy's psyche. To excise her completely would cause psychic scarring." This was a lie, and Lucien looked up from his scroll with a raised eyebrow, though the librarian wisely said nothing. "Therefore," Dream decreed, "I am ruling in favor of joint custody." "Joint—?" First Love choked. "You shall share the vessel," Dream said, gesturing vaguely with a pale hand. "First Love, you retain the meadow and the dialogue. Mora, you are granted visitation rights for the final three minutes of the REM cycle, twice weekly. You may sit on his chest and consume up to, but not exceeding, thirty percent of his breath." "A light snack," Mora mused, nodding. "I can work with that." "My Lord, no!" First Love pleaded. "What becomes of the avatar? What becomes of Chloe?" "You will merge the assets," Dream said, already standing up, his cloak billowing around him. "Chloe Miller will remain in the meadow, though she will now possess black sclera, a slight smell of peat moss, and an uncanny ability to unhinge her jaw when leaning in for a kiss." First Love looked as though he might faint. "You're going to give that poor boy very specific, very problematic tastes in women for the rest of his life." Dream paused at the threshold of the shadow that served as his exit. He looked back, his dark eyes glittering with a rare, dry amusement. "Yes," Dream said. "I suppose he will grow up to write poetry. Next case, Lucien."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the complex prompt requirements, successfully creating a courtroom drama within the Dreaming that balances dark fantasy with understated comedy. The author captures Dream's characterization well - his irritation, formality, and subtle mischievousness align with established depictions of the character. The voice remains consistent throughout, maintaining the dry, sardonic tone appropriate for both the setting and the absurd situation. The characterizations are particularly effective. First Love as a bashful, precious entity contrasts sharply with Mora's pragmatic, predatory nature. Their dialogue feels authentic to their mythological roles while serving the comedic premise. Dream's judicial weariness and subtle sadism come through clearly in both his dialogue and actions. The prose is generally elegant and restrained, avoiding purple excess while maintaining atmospheric quality. Phrases like "his dark coat pooling around the base of his throne like spilled ink" and "voice was the rustle of dry leaves" are evocative without being overwrought. The courtroom setting shifts subtly with the gallery's mood, adding texture without distraction. The comedy emerges naturally from the situation rather than forced jokes. Mora's defense of "a girl's gotta eat too" and her comparison of Ohio dreams to "chewing sawdust" land effectively. The absurdity of joint custody over a teenager's dreams, complete with specific breath-consumption percentages, maintains the dark humor throughout. However, there are some weaknesses. The ending, while clever, feels slightly rushed in its implications. The transformation of the boy's romantic development into something "problematic" could have been explored with more nuance. Some dialogue exchanges, particularly First Love's protests, occasionally veer toward exposition rather than natural speech. The piece succeeds in its primary goals: creating an engaging courtroom scene that feels authentic to the Dreaming while maintaining consistent dark comedy. Dream's mischievous resolution feels earned given his established character and the preceding irritation with bureaucratic matters. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 74.5
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A crimson harvest moon casts ominous shadows on the deserted village streets. The cobblestones of the medieval Bavarian town slicken with fresh blood, reflecting the bruised, scarlet glow of the sky. Shuttered windows rattle against a chill autumn wind, the surviving peasants cowering behind hex-marked doors. In the center of the town square stands Yennefer of Vengerberg. She brushes a speck of ash from her black velvet skirt, irritated. A portal malfunction—triggered by an unexpected geomagnetic anomaly—had dropped her into this backward sphere, right in the middle of a localized massacre. "Come out," she calls, her voice smooth, cold, and resonant. The scent of lilac and gooseberries cuts sharply through the heavy copper stench of slaughter. "I have little patience for theatrical lurking, and you've already ruined my boots." A low, rasping chuckle echoes from the bell tower, sliding down the timber-framed walls to pool in the darkness behind the stone fountain. The shadows there do not merely shift; they boil. Red eyes, glowing like dying embers, open within the gloom. "A witch," a deep, aristocratic voice purrs, layered with a thousand agonizing whispers. "And a remarkably arrogant one. Tell me, little sorceress, did you stumble into my dining room by accident, or are you the dessert?" From the blackness steps a tall, gaunt man. His attire is bizarre to her eyes—a sweeping crimson duster, a wide-brimmed hat, and strange, circular orange spectacles resting on a sharp nose. He holds two massive, gleaming metal contraptions in his white-gloved hands, their barrels smoking faintly. Yennefer’s violet eyes narrow. She is a master of magic, well-versed in the anatomy of higher vampires, bruxae, and katakans. Yet, looking at this creature, her stomach tightens with a visceral revulsion—and an undeniable, perilous fascination. He is not merely a monster; he is an abyss wrapped in the mockery of human skin. "I am nobody's dessert," Yennefer replies, her chin tilting upward. Chaos thrums in her veins, hot and eager, gathering at her fingertips. "And if this mess is your doing, you have appalling table manners." Alucard’s grin widens, splitting his pale face with an impossible number of gleaming, razor-sharp teeth. "Manners are for the living, my dear. The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." He raises the silver gun—the Casull—with casual lethality and pulls the trigger. The roar is deafening, a thunderclap of alchemical gunpowder. Yennefer barely has time to flick her wrist. A shimmering kinetic barrier snaps into existence an inch from her face. The massive silver bullet strikes the shield, flattening with a violent spark that illuminates her pale, furious features before ricocheting into a wooden tavern wall, splintering the oak. Alucard tilts his head, his orange glasses flashing in the blood-moonlight. "Fascinating. No incantation. Just pure, concentrated will." "You will find I am full of surprises," Yennefer hisses. She does not wait for a second shot. She slashes her hand through the air, speaking a sharp word in Elder Speech. A jagged bolt of white-hot lightning erupts from her palm, crossing the square in a fraction of a second. It strikes Alucard squarely in the chest, the concussive force blowing him backward through the stone basin of the fountain. Water, stone, and limbs scatter. His torso is charred, his left arm completely severed by the plasma-like heat. Yennefer steps forward, magic still crackling between her fingers, her breath steady. A lesser creature—even a Regis or a Dettlaff—would be incapacitated, forced into mist to regenerate over days or weeks. Instead, a sound bubbles up from the wreckage. It is laughter. Maniacal, delighted, and entirely unbothered. The shadows beneath the broken fountain writhe. Tendrils of dark, ocular matter lash out, seizing the severed arm and pulling it back to the ruined shoulder. Flesh knits together in seconds, bone snapping back into place with sickening cracks. Alucard rises from the rubble, dusting off his immaculate red coat, entirely whole. "Magnificent!" Alucard roars, spreading his arms wide. "It has been centuries since a mortal woman made my heart stop! Do it again, witch! Tear me apart!" Yennefer masks her sudden spike of alarm behind a sneer. "You're a masochist. How utterly tedious." Before she can weave another spell, he blurs. He does not teleport; he simply moves with a speed that defies physical law. Suddenly, he is towering over her, the stench of centuries-old grave dirt and dried blood overwhelming her senses. A massive, gloved hand—now sporting claws capable of rending steel—lunges for her throat. Yennefer drops backward into a shimmering tear in reality, a micro-portal snapping shut just as Alucard’s claws slice through the empty air where her jugular had been. She reappears twenty paces behind him, atop the steps of the village church. With a sweeping gesture, she rips the iron gates from the church archway, twisting the metal via telekinesis into a dozen razor-sharp lances. With a flick of her fingers, she launches them. Alucard doesn't bother to dodge. The iron spears impale him, pinning him to the cobblestones like a grotesque insect. Blood gushes from his mouth, dark and thick, yet his glowing eyes remain locked onto her, burning with predatory amusement. "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving," Yennefer says coldly, descending the steps, keeping a cautious distance. "Nor am I prey for a rabid dog who doesn't know when to die." "Die?" Alucard’s voice drops an octave, vibrating through the very stones beneath her boots. The iron spears pinning him begin to melt, consumed by a tide of pitch-black familiars—hellhounds and shadowy visages—bursting from his wounds. "Monsters do not die at the hands of monsters, Yennefer of Vengerberg." She freezes, her spine stiffening. "How do you know my name?" Alucard pulls himself free, his form shifting from a swarm of eyes and shadow back into the tall, dapper aristocrat. He taps the side of his head. "The blood in the air whispers, my dear. And your mind... it is a fortress, yes, bruised and rebuilt. I can smell the twisted spine you hid away with magic. I can taste the hollow ache in your womb." Rage, pure and blinding, flares in Yennefer’s violet eyes. The temperature in the square plummets, frost instantly coating the blood-slicked cobblestones. The air warps around her as she draws heavily from the intersections of elemental power, preparing a spell that will level the entire village if necessary. Alucard lowers his guns, holstering them beneath his coat. He removes his wide-brimmed hat and offers her a deep, mocking bow, exposing his neck in a blatant challenge. "Show me your worst, crooked little witch," Alucard whispers, his smile gleaming beneath the crimson moon. "Let us see whose eternity breaks first." Yennefer raises both hands, the blinding light of her magic colliding with the encroaching tide of his abyssal darkness, neither willing to yield an inch to the other.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and faithful character portrayal within a well-constructed supernatural encounter. The author successfully captures both characters' essential traits - Alucard's sadistic pleasure in combat and theatrical nature, and Yennefer's pride, magical prowess, and refusal to be intimidated. The medieval European setting is effectively established through atmospheric details like cobblestones, timber-framed buildings, and the village church. The combat sequences are particularly well-crafted, showcasing each character's abilities in escalating exchanges that feel authentic to their respective universes. Alucard's regenerative powers and shape-shifting are vividly portrayed, while Yennefer's magic feels appropriately powerful and varied. The power dynamic shifts naturally as requested, with neither character gaining clear dominance. The prose maintains consistent quality throughout, with strong imagery that creates a gothic atmosphere appropriate to both franchises. The blood moon setting provides effective symbolism and visual cohesion. Dialogue captures each character's voice well, incorporating their signature quotes naturally into the conversation. However, the piece occasionally veers toward purple prose, particularly in descriptions of violence and supernatural elements. Some metaphors feel overwrought ("abyss wrapped in the mockery of human skin"). The pacing rushes somewhat toward the end, and while the escalating conflict is engaging, it follows a fairly predictable pattern of attack-regenerate-counter-attack. The emotional complexity is present but could be deeper - Yennefer's "visceral revulsion and undeniable, perilous fascination" is mentioned but not fully explored. The piece succeeds as an action-focused encounter but doesn't delve as deeply into the psychological aspects of their interaction as it might. The ending feels appropriately unresolved, maintaining the tension without forcing a conclusion, though it's somewhat abrupt. Overall, this is competent fan fiction that respects both source materials while creating an engaging crossover scenario. + Fanfic-crossover: Prison Strings — Score: 79.5
Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A dim overhead light flickers in the prison corridor at irregular intervals, casting long, jagged shadows across the damp concrete of the Subterranean Containment Ward. This isn’t Green Dolphin Street Prison anymore. Whatever government black-site dragged Jolyne Cujoh down here deals in things far weirder than ordinary criminals. Footsteps echo down the hall—crisp, measured, and entirely out of place among the usual shuffling of inmates and heavy boots of guards. Jolyne leans against the reinforced steel bars of her cell, arms crossed over her chest, the butterfly tattoo on her forearm flexing as she narrows her eyes. A woman stops right outside her cell. She wears a pristine white dress shirt, a black tie, and dark slacks. Her auburn hair is braided neatly, and she smiles with a gentle, almost maternal warmth. It’s the eyes that set off every alarm bell in Jolyne’s head. Yellow, ringed like a target, and entirely devoid of life. "Good evening, Jolyne Cujoh," the woman says. Her voice is soft, pleasant, and utterly relaxing. "My name is Makima. I'm with Public Safety. I've been reviewing your file, and I must say, you've had a rather unfair run of luck." Jolyne doesn't uncross her arms. She spits onto the concrete floor near the bars. "Save the sweet talk, lady. Anyone who walks down here smiling like a Sunday school teacher is either crazy or looking to dissect me. What do you want?" Makima tilts her head slightly, her smile never wavering. "Perceptive. I like that. Most prisoners down here beg for their lives or try to make blind deals. You're different." She steps closer to the bars, clasps her hands behind her back, and peers at Jolyne. "The guards say you attacked three of them without ever leaving your bunk. No devil contracts. No biological anomalies. Just... invisible strings." Unseen by normal humans, a single, translucent blue thread is already creeping along the floor from Jolyne’s heel, sliding silently toward Makima’s ankle. "Maybe the guards are just clumsy," Jolyne mutters, her eyes locked onto Makima’s face. "Or maybe they pissed me off. You're getting pretty close to doing the same." Makima’s ringed eyes suddenly flick down, staring directly at the spot where Jolyne's Stand string is an inch away from her shoe. Jolyne’s breath hitches. *She can see it? Is she a Stand user?* "Fascinating," Makima murmurs, her tone mildly amused. "It smells like you. It's literally a piece of your soul unraveled, isn't it? Not a devil at all. Something born entirely of human willpower." "Back off!" Jolyne snaps. She flicks her wrist, and a dozen more threads shoot from her fingertips, weaving together instantly to wrap around Makima’s throat and wrists, yanking her violently against the steel bars. Makima doesn't gasp. She doesn't even flinch as the steel presses into her cheek and the razor-sharp strings dig into the skin of her neck, drawing a thin line of blood. She simply looks at Jolyne through the bars, her yellow eyes wide and unblinking. "I'm giving you three seconds to tell me who the hell you are and how you're getting me out of here," Jolyne growls, pulling the strings tighter. "Otherwise, Stone Free is gonna slice that pretty little neck of yours into ribbons." "You have a lot of spirit," Makima says, her voice completely unaffected by the constriction on her windpipe. "Like a stray dog that hasn't learned to heel yet. I find that quite endearing, Jolyne." "Call me a dog again, bitch. See what happens." "I can get you out of here right now," Makima continues smoothly. "I can clear your name, return you to your father, and erase every record of your crimes. All you have to do is belong to me." Then, Makima’s tone shifts. The warmth vanishes, replaced by an absolute, crushing authority. *"Release me, Jolyne. And sit."* A heavy, suffocating pressure slams into Jolyne’s mind. It feels like invisible chains wrapping around her brain, demanding obedience, telling her that the woman in front of her is superior in every conceivable way. Jolyne's knees buckle slightly. Her fingers twitch, almost slackening the strings. *What the hell is this?!* Jolyne grits her teeth so hard she thinks her molars might crack. *A Stand ability? Mind control?* Makima watches, waiting for the inevitable compliance. Humans always break. They are lesser creatures, meant to be guided on a leash. Instead, Jolyne glares up through her bangs, her eyes blazing with pure, unadulterated defiance. With a ferocious roar, she rips her own left forearm open using a jagged piece of her bunk's frame. Blood splatters onto the concrete. The sharp, blinding pain shatters the mental fog instantly. "Yare yare dawa..." Jolyne pants, wiping blood from her chin with the back of her hand, a feral smirk spreading across her face. "You really think some cheap hypnotic bullshit is gonna work on me? I don't take orders from anyone!" *"Stone Free!"* The blue, humanoid manifestation of her Stand bursts forth from the tangled strings, sunglasses gleaming under the flickering corridor light. *"ORA!"* Stone Free’s fist slams directly into Makima’s face through the gap in the bars. The impact sounds like a cannon shot. Makima’s head snaps back at an unnatural angle, the bridge of her nose shattering, and she is launched backward into the far wall of the corridor. She slumps to the floor in a heap, blood pooling beneath her. Jolyne breathes heavily, recalling Stone Free, though she keeps her strings coiled tightly around her fists. "Freak," she mutters, clutching her bleeding arm. The overhead light flickers out completely for two seconds. When it buzzes back on, the blood on the floor is gone. Makima is standing upright, dusting off her black slacks. Her nose is completely healed, her white shirt pristine once more. Somewhere in Japan, a random citizen just died of a sudden cranial impact, absorbing the fatal blow meant for the Control Devil. Jolyne’s eyes widen in genuine shock. "What... how did you—" Makima raises her right hand, forming her fingers into the shape of a gun, pointing her index finger directly at Jolyne’s chest. Her face is entirely blank, the mask of sweet civility dropped in favor of cold, calculated dominance. "You really are a bad dog, Jolyne," Makima says softly. "It seems I'll have to break your legs before we talk about the collar." *"Bang."*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This story demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt, successfully capturing both characters' essential traits and creating a compelling supernatural prison encounter. The author effectively portrays Jolyne's hot-headed defiance and Makima's manipulative nature, building tension through their psychological battle. The characterization is particularly strong. Jolyne's immediate suspicion, foul-mouthed dialogue ("Save the sweet talk, lady"), and refusal to submit feel authentic to her character. Her self-harm to break Makima's mental control is a believable desperate measure that showcases her fierce independence. Makima's false sweetness masking cold calculation is well-executed, especially in the transition from maternal warmth to commanding authority. The prose maintains a consistent dark, tense atmosphere throughout. Descriptive elements like the flickering light, "ringed yellow eyes," and the supernatural prison setting create effective mood without becoming overwrought. The action sequences are clearly written and easy to follow. Dialogue feels natural and character-appropriate. Jolyne's crude defiance ("Call me a dog again, bitch") contrasts effectively with Makima's measured manipulation. The power dynamics are well-established through their verbal sparring. The story builds tension effectively, escalating from suspicion to direct confrontation. Makima's regeneration and the revelation of her true nature creates a strong cliffhanger ending that feels earned rather than cheap. However, some elements feel slightly predictable - the immediate mutual antagonism and escalation to violence follows expected patterns. The Stand ability explanation could have been more seamlessly integrated. Some descriptions border on purple prose ("razor-sharp strings dig into the skin") but don't cross into overwrought territory. The pacing is tight and the 1000-word constraint is well-managed, though this leaves some character depth unexplored. The ending maintains the dark tone appropriately without false positivity. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 87.5
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-7841 **Object Class:** Euclid (Provisional) **Special Containment Procedures:** As SCP-7841 is entirely localized to my person, I, Dr. Arthur Vance, have been placed in a standard High-Security Humanoid Containment Cell at Site-19. All stationery, writing implements, and standard Foundation memo pads within a fifty-meter radius have been incinerated. My quarters are monitored via 24-hour closed-circuit television, and I am required to undergo daily evaluations with Site-19’s Psychiatric Division and the Department of Temporal Anomalies. I am dictating this report via voice-to-text software. I am not allowed to hold a pen. **Description:** SCP-7841 is an ongoing phenomenon in which handwritten notes, composed on standard 10cm x 15cm yellow Foundation memo paper, materialize in my immediate vicinity. Forensics has confirmed that the handwriting, ink pressure, and trace skin oil deposits on these pages are a 100% match to my own. However, the content of the notes suggests they are being transmitted from a point in the immediate future. The anomaly began on October 12th. I arrived at my office in Sector-4, poured a cup of coffee, and found the first note resting on my keyboard. > *Arthur. Don’t file the requisition for the beryllium-bronze plating on 4092’s cell. The shipment is compromised. It’s going to blow the sub-level on the 19th. Just cancel the order. Trust me, I’m you. Check your left collarbone—you burned it with the soldering iron in 1998. Cancel the order.* At first, I assumed it was a prank by Junior Researcher Meyers, though the collarbone detail gave me pause. I reported the breach of my office security to Site Command. While we were reviewing the hallway camera footage—which showed no one entering my office all night—I reached into my lab coat pocket for my keycard and pulled out a second yellow slip. > *You went to Security. Idiot. Now they’re going to quarantine you and the order will go through automatically. Tell Director Vance to override Protocol 12. The breach starts in Sector-4. The walls are bleeding.* That was the first discrepancy. The Director of Site-19 is Laura Dietz. There has never been a Director Vance. Furthermore, there is no SCP-4092 housed at Site-19; that designation belongs to a safe-class toaster kept in a locker at Site-77. By October 14th, I was placed in observation. The Department of Temporal Anomalies set up Kant counters around my desk to measure local reality fluctuations. The needles didn't budge. Because of this, Dr. Glass from Psychiatry hypothesized that SCP-7841 was not a temporal anomaly at all, but a localized cognitohazard or telepathic manipulation generated by an existing Euclid-class entity in Sector-4. They suspected I was entering fugue states and writing the notes myself. To test this, I locked my only pad of Foundation memo paper inside a heavy-duty steel safe in the observation room, set a randomized twelve-digit combination, and swallowed the backup key. I sat on my hands under the glare of four high-speed cameras. Three hours later, I coughed violently. I spat a wad of damp, yellow paper onto the sterile floor. The cameras showed it hadn't been in my mouth a millisecond prior. > *The air scrubbers failed an hour ago. Why didn't you listen? It’s in the vents. It smells like copper and lilacs. Meyers is gone, it wore his skin like a suit, Arthur, it wore him and it smiled at me. Don’t let them open the red door in the basement. Site-19 doesn't have a basement, why is there a basement? Lock the safe, it’s coming through the paper.* When the guards retrieved the note, they also opened the steel safe to check the control pad. One sheet had been torn from the top. I began to doubt my own mind. It is a terrifying thing, to look at your own frantic scrawl and feel no connection to the terror that produced it. I found myself sniffing the air, terrified I would catch the scent of lilacs. Every time Junior Researcher Meyers walked past my observation window, I stared at the seams of his neck, looking for a zipper, a tear, a sign that he wasn't real. Dr. Glass told me that my cortisol levels were lethal. He suggested amnestics to "reset" whatever memetic agent had latched onto my cortex. I agreed. On October 17th, they prepped the Class-A gaseous compound. As the technician raised the mask to my face, a note manifested directly between my corneas and the inside of my glasses, blinding me. > *NO AMNESTICS. IF YOU FORGET, YOU LET IT IN. IT NEEDS YOU BLANK. THE BREACH ISN'T AN OBJECT, ARTHUR, IT'S AN IDEA. IT'S EATING THE TIMELINE FROM THE FORWARD END BACK. THE SKY IS GONE. THE SUN IS A HOLE. BREAK YOUR FINGERS SO YOU CAN'T WRITE IT DOWN.* I panicked. I thrashed against my restraints, shattering my glasses and screaming until my vocal cords tore. The handwriting on that note was barely legible—a jagged, tearing scrawl that had ripped through the yellow paper in several places. Forensics found traces of dried blood mixed with the ballpoint ink. My blood. Since yesterday, October 18th, the notes have been arriving every twenty minutes. They materialize inside my shoes, under my tongue, and folded inside the seams of my standard-issue jumpsuit. All memo pads in the facility were burned this morning, yet the notes still arrive on that same cheap, lined yellow paper, smelling faintly of wood pulp and ozone. The contradictions are getting worse. The notes reference colleagues who died years ago, containment wings that were never built, and a version of the Foundation that seems to be at war with the concept of geometry itself. Here is the final note I received, ten minutes ago, found wedged beneath my fingernails: > *It’s the 19th. It’s here. It wasn't a breach. We aren't keeping it locked out, Arthur. We’re keeping it locked in with us. You're writing the report right now. Stop dictating. It travels through the documentation. Once you classify it, it becomes real. Don't finish the file. Don't give it a number. Please, I'm sorry, I'm so sorry, I have to write these so you'll put them in the system. It's making me hold the pen.* I am looking at the microphone right now. The red recording light is blinking. My hands are empty, resting on the metal table, completely still. Wait. My right index finger is stained with blue ink. And the air in my cell is starting to smell like lilacs.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP report demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of the Foundation universe while delivering a genuinely unsettling psychological horror story. The author successfully captures the clinical, bureaucratic tone characteristic of SCP documentation while gradually subverting it as the anomaly takes hold. The piece excels in its structural approach, using the format of an official report to create mounting dread. The integration of the handwritten notes as both plot device and source of horror is particularly effective, with each note escalating the tension while introducing reality-distorting elements. The progression from mundane security concerns to existential terror feels organic and well-paced. The characterization of Dr. Vance is believable and nuanced. His rational, scientific approach gradually gives way to paranoia and desperation in a psychologically convincing manner. The author effectively shows his deteriorating mental state through his observations and reactions rather than simply stating his fear. The horror elements are genuinely creative, particularly the concept of an entity that "travels through documentation" and the implication that the very act of filing the report enables the breach. This meta-textual element adds layers to the horror without feeling gimmicky. The contradictory information in the notes (Director Vance, non-existent SCPs, impossible architecture) creates effective cognitive dissonance. The prose maintains clinical precision while building atmospheric dread. Specific details like "smelling faintly of wood pulp and ozone" and "the seams of his neck" create vivid, unsettling imagery. The ending is particularly strong, with the revelation about the ink stain and lilac scent providing a chilling conclusion that suggests the cycle is beginning anew. The piece adheres closely to the prompt requirements, maintaining first-person perspective, past tense, and incorporating all requested elements including the Foundation's investigation methods and the researcher's psychological struggle. The length constraint is well-managed, with no section feeling rushed or underdeveloped. Minor weaknesses include some exposition that borders on telling rather than showing, particularly in explaining the Foundation's testing procedures, though this is somewhat mitigated by the clinical report format which naturally accommodates such information.
